headline: Mitsubishi UFJ: half-year profit up 26% on rising Japanese rates; full-year target raised to ¥2.8 trillion and dividend to ¥100
takeaway: Profit for the six months to September rose 26% to ¥1.63 trillion, driven by a 29% jump in net interest income as the Bank of Japan’s rate increases flowed through. MUFG raised its full-year profit target to ¥2.8 trillion and its dividend forecast to ¥100 a share, yet the ADRs slipped 2.5% on the day.
results: Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group reported profit attributable to shareholders of ¥1,630.9 billion for the six months ended September 30, up 26.1%. Ordinary profit rose 29.4% to ¥2,261.0 billion and earnings per share rose to ¥144.73 from ¥113.07. In dollar terms the second quarter came to about US$0.46 per ADS against a consensus of roughly US$0.45.

At the two main subsidiaries, net interest income rose ¥411 billion, or 29%, to ¥1,851 billion, net fees and commissions rose 14% to ¥1,138 billion and trading profits nearly tripled. Against that, the bank booked ¥196 billion of losses on bond sales, and general and administrative expenses rose 11%. Net operating profit before credit costs rose 25% to ¥1,639 billion.

Total assets were ¥425.8 trillion and shareholders’ equity ¥22.8 trillion. The interim dividend was ¥48, up from ¥35 a year earlier, and the full-year forecast was raised to ¥100 from ¥86 paid last year.
mgmt: MUFG does not publish a conventional earnings forecast; it sets a profit target and explained again that market and economic uncertainty make a forecast impractical. The target for the year to March 2027 is now ¥2.8 trillion, changed from the figure set in May. The half-year result already represents 58% of that target.

The company also revised its dividend forecast, putting the second-half payment at ¥52 for a total of ¥100. Management linked the improvement mainly to higher yen interest rates, stronger fee income across its banking, trust and securities businesses and better results at its overseas operations.
view: For three decades the story of Japanese banks was that they could not make money: zero rates crushed lending margins and investors valued them at a fraction of book value. This half-year is evidence that the story has changed. A 29% increase in net interest income in six months comes almost entirely from the Bank of Japan moving rates off zero; every increment flows straight through on ¥200-odd trillion of yen deposits that cost the bank close to nothing. MUFG is now earning a return on equity in the low teens, a level that would have been unimaginable in 2020.

The bond losses are worth understanding rather than fearing. MUFG is selling low-yielding government bonds bought when rates were near zero and reinvesting at higher yields. That costs money now and lifts income later, and the bank can afford it because core profits are rising so fast. Combined with a 16% dividend increase and the bank’s habit of announcing buybacks with its results, the capital story is as strong as the earnings story.

The muted reaction says much of this is priced in. The shares have rerated from about half of book value to well above it, and the next leg depends on how far the Bank of Japan goes. If rates rise toward 1.5%, the earnings power is materially higher again; if growth stalls and the central bank pauses, the market will focus on credit costs and MUFG’s large exposure to Morgan Stanley, Indonesian and Thai lending. On the evidence of this report, management is setting conservative targets and beating them.
watch: Watch the Bank of Japan’s next rate decision, the size of any new share buyback at the full-year results in May, and whether bond-sale losses keep growing as the bank repositions its securities book.
